blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
blocks.zh: 视觉-语言模型(VLMs)与RGB观察中仍然隐含的度量和多视图关系相抗衡. 几何地基模型从RGB中恢复了这种结构,但现有方法要么将估计的地物与可视地物相接并学会单独从问答中加以使用,要么将VLM潜入物与几何地物相接. 然而,捕捉几何并不能确保它的使用: 将释放的地物-对齐模型的对齐潜想零出,使其精度保持不变. 我们介绍GeoReader,这个框架为读取它们的VLM学习几何表达. 首先,我们训练轻量级几何读取器来制作连续的输入符号,用被被冷冻的VLM解码的几何描述来监督它们,使读者以目标模型已经能读取的形式来表达几何. 然后我们冻结了读者来保存这个接口,同时在空间QA上微调了VLM,这个问题上有几何注射条件. 几何描述只作为训练目标:推论VLM直接从连续几何符号中解答,而不产生几何思维链. 根据RGB图像的几何预测,我们的方法在MindCube-Tiny上与Quen3-VL-4B并用,在多源QA混合物下,平均达到72.5分6个额外的空间基准并用Quen3.5-9B. 这些结果表明,有用的几何表示是接收模型可以使用的一种,而不仅仅是可以重建几何的表示.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated increasingly strong
capabilities in general multimodal understanding, yet continue to struggle with
spatial reasoning, a capability essential to embodied intelligence in the 3D
world [ Li et al., 2025a ; Hu et al., 2026a ] . A central challenge is inferring and reasoning about 3D structure from
2D observations [ Li et al., 2025b ] , as required by spatial questions involving camera motion,
viewpoint changes, and object distances. Recent advances in geometry foundation
models [ Wang et al., 2025a ; Lin et al., 2026 ] offer a promising opportunity to address
this limitation by providing geometry information. How to harness
this information for VLM spatial reasoning has
therefore become an important question.

blocks.en:
Existing approaches to integrating geometry foundation models with VLMs have
improved spatial reasoning and can be broadly categorized into two streams. The
first introduces geometry as an additional input
modality [ Fan et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2026 ] , fusing features from geometry foundation models with the VLM’s original visual features ( Fig. 1 a). This provides a direct way to incorporate geometry into existing VLMs,
and the VLM learns to use these features from downstream supervision.
However, this supervision alone may not teach the VLM to
interpret geometry features. The second uses geometry
as supervision, typically by aligning VLM latent representations with features from geometry foundation models [ Chen et al., 2026 ] ( Fig. 1 b). This encourages the
latent space to capture geometry information while preserving the VLM’s input
and output interfaces. Nevertheless, capturing geometry does not ensure its use: zeroing the latents of the released first-stage 3DThinker [ Chen et al., 2026 ] checkpoint leaves MindCube-Tiny [ Wang et al., 2026a ] accuracy essentially unchanged, and answer tokens barely attend to them ( ; ).
Related analyses of latent visual reasoning methods such as
LVR [ Li et al., 2026a ] and Monet [ Wang et al., 2026b ] also highlight a
disconnect between intermediate representations and answer
generation [ Viveiros et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026d ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ] .
Despite their differences, neither approach explicitly bridges the gap between
geometry representations and language-grounded spatial relations for VLMs.
Consequently, the role of geometry information in the model’s reasoning remains
uncertain. We bridge this gap by converting geometry into a form that VLMs can both interpret and ground in language.

blocks.en:
We introduce Geo Reader , based on the core idea that geometry should first be converted into a form that VLMs can interpret as spatial relationships in language, before VLMs learn to use it for downstream tasks . To this end, a two-stage pipeline separates adapting geometry to the VLM from applying it to spatial QA ( Fig. 1 c). In Stage 1,
we train lightweight Geometric Readers to convert per-view geometric signals
into continuous geometric tokens. These tokens and the corresponding images are given to a frozen VLM that predicts geometry descriptions. With
the VLM frozen, this supervision trains the Readers to express geometry
information in a form that the model can interpret through its existing
language capabilities. In Stage 2, we transfer the pretrained Readers to spatial QA, freezing the Readers to preserve their learned mapping while fine-tuning the VLM to use their outputs. Since
questions differ in how much they rely on each geometric signal, a geometry injector conditions on the images and question to set each signal’s strength. Geometry descriptions are used only for Stage 1
supervision; at inference, the VLM answers directly using the geometric tokens.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion

blocks.en:
We presented Geo Reader , which converts geometry into a form that a frozen VLM
can read before the VLM learns to use it. Geometric Readers learn through
geometry-description prediction by the frozen VLM, then stay frozen while the
VLM and a question-conditioned geometry injector learn spatial QA;
descriptions serve only as training targets. Zeroing the aligned latents of a
released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged, whereas removing Geo Reader ’s geometry lowers it. With geometry predicted from RGB, Geo Reader reaches 94.3 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and a six-benchmark average

blocks.en:
The Panel B alternatives in follow the MindCube
ablation setting of Sec. A.2.3 with answer-only
supervision. The two adapted fusion rows use pre-extracted final-layer
VGGT [ Wang et al., 2025a ] features from the input RGB images: one camera token
and 1,369 patch tokens per view, each 2,048-dimensional; the four register
tokens are excluded. The VGGT and Qwen visual encoders are frozen, while the
full language model and fusion module are trained with QA answer loss. Both
fusion modules use per-frame cross-attention with a 512-dimensional attention
space and eight heads. They modify the Qwen image embeddings before one LLM
pass, without adding geometric tokens to the input or using a Geometric Reader.

Following the spatial–visual fusion idea of VLM-3R [ Fan et al., 2026 ] , each
frame’s Qwen image embeddings query that frame’s VGGT camera and patch
features. A learned output projection maps the attended features back to the
Qwen hidden dimension, and its zero-initialized residual is added to the
corresponding image embeddings. We adopt only the fusion mechanism; the
original VLM-3R system uses CUT3R [ Wang et al., 2025b ] features.

帧的 Quen 图像嵌入了 帧的 VGGT 相机和补丁 查询
特性。 学习到的输出投影图
将 Quen 隐藏维度及其零初始残基添加到
相应的图像嵌入。 我们只采用聚变机制;

Inspired by the camera-guided fusion of SpaceMind [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] ,
we retain the same per-frame visual queries and VGGT features but use the
